A globular enzyme binds substrate at an active site, forms an enzyme–substrate complex and releases products while remaining available for reuse.
Space-filling models show hexokinase changing conformation around glucose during catalysis.
Energy profiles and a boulder analogy compare catalysed and uncatalysed routes. Reactant and product energy levels stay the same; the catalysed activation barrier is lower.
Enzyme-controlled steps link substrates and products in linear, branched and cyclic metabolic pathways. Cycles regenerate an intermediate while still exchanging matter and energy.

The textbook compares active-site competition with binding at another site, alongside illustrative substrate-concentration curves. The pure non-competitive curve is a simplified model, not a rule for every allosteric inhibitor.
An accumulating pathway end product feeds back to inhibit an early enzyme, reducing unnecessary further synthesis.
Penicillin binds DD-transpeptidase and prevents peptide cross-links from forming between peptidoglycan chains.
Motor, relay and sensory neurons show cell bodies, dendrites, axons and impulse direction. Enlargements show Schwann-cell wrapping, myelin and nodes of Ranvier.

An arriving impulse triggers calcium entry and vesicle exocytosis. Neurotransmitter diffuses across the cleft and binds postsynaptic receptors. A second panel shows acetylcholine breakdown and recycling.

Sodium and potassium channels accompany a membrane-potential trace labelled resting potential, depolarization, repolarization and hyperpolarization. Potassium-channel opening, rather than sodium–potassium pumping, produces rapid repolarization.

Drawings and micrographs show prophase, metaphase, anaphase, telophase and cytokinesis, with the spindle, chromosomes and nuclear envelope. Follow the arrows for the phase sequence; the drawing simplifies chromosome number.
A receptor detects a change, a coordinator processes the information and an effector opposes the deviation. Feedback reduces the response as conditions return towards the regulated range.
Opposing feedback loops connect pancreatic alpha cells and glucagon with a rise in blood glucose, and beta cells and insulin with a fall in blood glucose.
High temperature activates sweating and skin vasodilation. Low temperature activates shivering and vasoconstriction. Each response opposes the original temperature change.

The glomerulus and Bowman’s capsule show afferent/efferent arterioles, the filtration barrier and a podocyte micrograph. Small solutes enter filtrate while blood cells and most plasma proteins remain in blood.

Apical microvilli, basal infoldings and mitochondria support reabsorption. Basolateral sodium–potassium pumps help drive sodium-coupled solute uptake, with reabsorbed substances returning to capillaries.
Side-by-side diagrams compare low and high ADH. More permeable collecting ducts allow greater water reabsorption into the concentrated medulla, producing less, more concentrated urine.
Bronchioles lead to alveoli surrounded by capillaries. A section and photomicrograph show the thin air–blood diffusion barrier, red blood cells and the capillary network.
Haemoglobin structure is shown beside a sigmoid oxygen dissociation curve relating percentage saturation to oxygen partial pressure.
The foetal haemoglobin curve is left of the adult curve, indicating greater saturation at the same intermediate oxygen partial pressure.
Higher carbon dioxide shifts haemoglobin’s oxygen dissociation curve right, promoting oxygen unloading at the same oxygen partial pressure in actively respiring tissue.
A transverse-section micrograph and labelled drawings compare arteries and veins using wall thickness, smooth muscle, elastic fibres and lumen size.
Bony-fish blood passes through gills then body before returning to the heart. Mammalian blood returns to the heart between pulmonary and systemic capillary beds.
External and frontal-section views label chambers, major vessels, valves and the muscular wall. Anatomical left and right refer to the patient, not the viewer.
Mineral-ion uptake lowers water potential in the xylem. Water enters by osmosis, generating positive hydrostatic pressure.
An electron micrograph and interpretive drawing identify Z lines, actin, myosin and the light and dark bands of a sarcomere.
Micrographs and drawings compare relaxed and contracted sarcomeres: Z lines approach and filament overlap increases while the filaments retain their lengths.
A branching motor neuron ends in several motor end plates. Enlargements show axon, Schwann-cell myelin and nodes. A motor neuron and all fibres it innervates form a motor unit.
The motor-neuron terminal contains vesicles and mitochondria and faces the folded muscle sarcolemma across a synaptic cleft.
Condensation joins monomers and releases water. Hydrolysis consumes water to split the linkage. Arrows show the opposite reaction directions.
Six-carbon glucose and five-carbon ribose are shown in structural formulae, including carbon atoms outside each ring and alpha/beta glucose orientations.
Alternating beta-glucose residues form straight chains. Hydrogen bonds connect neighbouring cellulose chains into fibrils and fibres that resist tension.
Amylose is an unbranched alpha-glucose polymer. Amylopectin has alpha-1,4 linkages along its chains and alpha-1,6 linkages at branch points.
Three fatty acids form ester linkages with glycerol by condensation, releasing three water molecules overall.
Hydrophilic phospholipid heads contact water while hydrophobic tails face away. The arrangement forms monolayers or bilayers according to the interface.
Testosterone and oestradiol share the characteristic four fused carbon rings of steroid molecules.

The diagram compares amino-acid sequence, local secondary folding, overall tertiary conformation and the association of polypeptide subunits in quaternary structure. Active sites are a feature of enzymes, not every protein.
Length, banding pattern and centromere position are labelled as the three features used to match homologous chromosomes.
Early development, embryonic stem cells and adult stem cells illustrate the narrowing range of possible cell fates: totipotent, pluripotent and multipotent.
Cells including erythrocytes, leukocytes, epithelial cells, sperm, an oocyte, neurons and a muscle fibre have their dimensions listed. Drawings are explicitly not to a common scale.
A nerve cutaway shows axons within fascicles, connective-tissue coverings, blood vessels, myelin and nodes. A nerve contains many neuronal fibres.

A sensory neuron carries information from the stimulated hand to the spinal cord. A relay neuron connects to a motor neuron and a muscle contracts to withdraw the hand; signals also travel to the brain.
T and t denote tall and dwarf pea plants. Parental gametes, heterozygous F1 plants and an F2 Punnett grid illustrate a 1:2:1 genotype ratio and 3:1 phenotype ratio with complete dominance.
Heterozygous group-A and group-B parents can produce offspring with groups A, B, AB and O. A and B alleles are codominant; both dominate O.

The pea cross uses R/r for shape and Y/y for colour. Four gamete types from each RrYy parent form a sixteen-cell grid with a 9:3:3:1 phenotype ratio under independent assortment and complete dominance.
Homologous chromosomes carry linked loci. Crossing over between non-sister chromatids can create new allele combinations; parental and recombinant gametes and offspring are distinguished.
Trait-frequency distributions before and after selection show a shift towards one extreme, concentration around the middle or the favouring of both extremes.
Pioneers, soil development and later vegetation illustrate a possible primary succession. The original figure states that this is not a rigid universal progression.

RNA is enclosed by a labelled phospholipid membrane in a model of compartmentalization and internal chemistry. This is a hypothesis, not a photograph or a diagram of the simpler fatty-acid vesicles discussed separately.
Two beetle communities have the same three species but different relative abundances. Equal richness can accompany different diversity because evenness differs.
An abiotic gradient passes through zones of intolerance, physiological stress and optimum conditions. Species differ in their tolerance limits; this is a model.
Biome regions are plotted against mean annual temperature vertically and precipitation horizontally. These generalized biome boundaries overlap in nature.
Arrows connect organisms being eaten to their consumers, indicating transfer of biomass and chemical energy. This marine example is distinct from the constructed meadow practice example.
Plant cells in hypotonic, isotonic and hypertonic solutions show turgidity, loss of turgor and plasmolysis. The cell wall stays outside the retracting protoplast.
The system diagram links greenhouse gases, warming, evaporation, ocean warming and reduced carbon-dioxide solubility, showing amplification of an initial warming.

Aligned panels show FSH, LH, oestradiol, progesterone, follicle development, ovulation and endometrial changes in an illustrative 28-day cycle. The LH surge precedes ovulation; real cycle lengths vary.
